question: Find the normative text (MUST, SHOULD, may, defaults, numbers) that decides each side of a comparison of Head-of-Line (HOL) blocking in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3: RFC 9113 (TCP-level HOL, frame processing order, HPACK state, field block contiguity, CONTINUATION, flow-control defaults); RFC 9000 (delivery guarantees within and across streams, effect of loss on other streams, stream and connection flow-control limits, receiver buffering); RFC 9114 (HOL compared with HTTP/2, critical streams, closed control stream); RFC 9204 (when QPACK blocks a stream, SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS default and encoder duty, encoder-stream blocking, avoiding blocking); RFC 7541 only for why decoding depends on header-block order.

facts.summary: RFC 9113 states that HTTP/2 does not address head-of-line blocking at the TCP layer.
facts.quote: Note, however, that TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed by this protocol.

facts.summary: HTTP/1.1 request pipelining only partly solved request concurrency and still has application-layer head-of-line blocking.
facts.quote: HTTP/1.1 [HTTP/1.1] added request pipelining, but this only partially addressed request concurrency and still suffers from application-layer head-of-line blocking.

facts.summary: In HTTP/2 the order frames are sent in matters: recipients process frames in the order received, and HEADERS/DATA order is semantically significant.
facts.quote: The order in which frames are sent is significant. Recipients process frames in the order they are received. In particular, the order of HEADERS and DATA frames is semantically significant.

facts.summary: A field block is processed as one unit and MUST be sent as a contiguous run of frames, with no frames of another type or stream interleaved.
facts.quote: Each field block is processed as a discrete unit. Field blocks MUST be transmitted as a contiguous sequence of frames, with no interleaved frames of any other type or from any other stream.

facts.summary: Because HEADERS, PUSH_PROMISE and CONTINUATION carry data that changes the receiver's compression context, a receiver must decompress every field block even for discarded frames; not decompressing, or a decoding error, is a connection error of type COMPRESSION_ERROR.
facts.quote: Field block fragments can only be sent as the frame payload of HEADERS, PUSH_PROMISE, or CONTINUATION frames because these frames carry data that can modify the compression context maintained by a receiver. An endpoint receiving HEADERS, PUSH_PROMISE, or CONTINUATION frames needs to reassemble field blocks and perform decompression even if the frames are to be discarded. A receiver MUST terminate the connection with a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type COMPRESSION_ERROR if it does not decompress a field block. … A decoding error in a field block MUST be treated as a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type COMPRESSION_ERROR.

facts.summary: HPACK compression is stateful: each endpoint has one encoder context and one decoder context shared by all field blocks on the connection.
facts.quote: Field compression is stateful. Each endpoint has an HPACK encoder context and an HPACK decoder context that are used for encoding and decoding all field blocks on a connection.

facts.summary: A HEADERS frame without END_HEADERS MUST be followed by a CONTINUATION frame on the same stream; any other frame, or a frame on another stream, is a connection error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.
facts.quote: A HEADERS frame without the END_HEADERS flag set MUST be followed by a CONTINUATION frame for the same stream. A receiver MUST treat the receipt of any other type of frame or a frame on a different stream as a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.

facts.summary: Multiplexing streams over one TCP connection creates contention and blocked streams; HTTP/2 flow control applies both per stream and to the whole connection.
facts.quote: Using streams for multiplexing introduces contention over use of the TCP connection, resulting in blocked streams. A flow-control scheme ensures that streams on the same connection do not destructively interfere with each other. Flow control is used for both individual streams and the connection as a whole.

facts.summary: HTTP/2 flow control is a credit-based scheme in which receivers advertise, through WINDOW_UPDATE frames, how many octets they will accept per stream and per connection.
facts.quote: Flow control is based on WINDOW_UPDATE frames. Receivers advertise how many octets they are prepared to receive on a stream and for the entire connection. This is a credit-based scheme.

facts.summary: New streams and the connection both start with a flow-control window of 65,535 octets; SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE changes only the per-stream initial value, and the connection window changes only through WINDOW_UPDATE.
facts.quote: When an HTTP/2 connection is first established, new streams are created with an initial flow-control window size of 65,535 octets. The connection flow-control window is also 65,535 octets. Both endpoints can adjust the initial window size for new streams by including a value for SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE in the SETTINGS frame. The connection flow-control window can only be changed using WINDOW_UPDATE frames.

facts.summary: Only DATA frames are subject to HTTP/2 flow control; other frame types consume no window space, so control frames are not blocked by flow control.
facts.quote: Of the frames specified in this document, only DATA frames are subject to flow control; all other frame types do not consume space in the advertised flow-control window. This ensures that important control frames are not blocked by flow control.

facts.summary: A sender MUST NOT send a flow-controlled frame larger than the space left in either the stream window or the connection window.
facts.quote: The sender MUST NOT send a flow-controlled frame with a length that exceeds the space available in either of the flow-control windows advertised by the receiver.

facts.summary: A flow-control window MUST NOT exceed 2^31-1 octets (the saved page renders the superscript as "231-1"); a WINDOW_UPDATE that pushes past it ends the stream or the connection.
facts.quote: A sender MUST NOT allow a flow-control window to exceed 231-1 octets. If a sender receives a WINDOW_UPDATE that causes a flow-control window to exceed this maximum, it MUST terminate either the stream or the connection, as appropriate.

facts.summary: Endpoints MUST read and process HTTP/2 frames from the TCP receive buffer as soon as data is available, since late reading can deadlock on unread WINDOW_UPDATE frames.
facts.quote: Endpoints MUST read and process HTTP/2 frames from the TCP receive buffer as soon as data is available. Failure to read promptly could lead to a deadlock when critical frames, such as WINDOW_UPDATE, are not read and acted upon.

facts.summary: RFC 9113 leaves to implementations how to avoid head-of-line blocking for requests, along with prioritization and stream creation.
facts.quote: Implementations are also responsible for prioritizing the sending of requests and responses, choosing how to avoid head-of-line blocking for requests, and managing the creation of new streams.

facts.summary: QUIC streams give the application an ordered byte-stream abstraction, either unidirectional or bidirectional.
facts.quote: Streams in QUIC provide a lightweight, ordered byte-stream abstraction to an application. Streams can be unidirectional or bidirectional.

facts.summary: Streams send data interleaved with other streams, and QUIC gives no ordering guarantee between bytes on different streams.
facts.quote: Streams can be created by either endpoint, can concurrently send data interleaved with other streams, and can be canceled. QUIC does not provide any means of ensuring ordering between bytes on different streams.

facts.summary: A receiver uses the Stream ID and Offset fields of STREAM frames to put data in order.
facts.quote: STREAM frames (Section 19.8) encapsulate data sent by an application. An endpoint uses the Stream ID and Offset fields in STREAM frames to place data in order.

facts.summary: Endpoints MUST be able to deliver each stream as an ordered byte stream, which requires buffering out-of-order data up to the advertised flow-control limit.
facts.quote: Endpoints MUST be able to deliver stream data to an application as an ordered byte stream. Delivering an ordered byte stream requires that an endpoint buffer any data that is received out of order, up to the advertised flow control limit.

facts.summary: QUIC makes no specific provision for out-of-order delivery of stream data, but implementations MAY offer it to the application.
facts.quote: QUIC makes no specific allowances for delivery of stream data out of order. However, implementations MAY choose to offer the ability to deliver data out of order to a receiving application.

facts.summary: On packet loss only the streams with data in the lost packet wait for retransmission; if one packet carried several streams, all of them are blocked, so implementations are advised to put as few streams per packet as efficiency allows.
facts.quote: One of the benefits of QUIC is avoidance of head-of-line blocking across multiple streams. When a packet loss occurs, only streams with data in that packet are blocked waiting for a retransmission to be received, while other streams can continue making progress. Note that when data from multiple streams is included in a single QUIC packet, loss of that packet blocks all those streams from making progress. Implementations are advised to include as few streams as necessary in outgoing packets without losing transmission efficiency to underfilled packets.

facts.summary: QUIC has two levels of limit-based flow control, per stream and per connection, and senders MUST NOT exceed either limit.
facts.quote: QUIC employs a limit-based flow control scheme where a receiver advertises the limit of total bytes it is prepared to receive on a given stream or for the entire connection. … Stream flow control, which prevents a single stream from consuming the entire receive buffer for a connection by limiting the amount of data that can be sent on each stream. … Connection flow control, which prevents senders from exceeding a receiver's buffer capacity for the connection by limiting the total bytes of stream data sent in STREAM frames on all streams. … Senders MUST NOT send data in excess of either limit.

facts.summary: MAX_STREAM_DATA carries the maximum absolute byte offset for one stream; MAX_DATA carries the maximum of the sum of absolute byte offsets over all streams.
facts.quote: A MAX_STREAM_DATA frame indicates the maximum absolute byte offset of a stream. … A receiver can advertise a larger limit for a connection by sending a MAX_DATA frame, which indicates the maximum of the sum of the absolute byte offsets of all streams.

facts.summary: A receiver MUST close the connection with FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR when the sender exceeds the connection or stream data limit.
facts.quote: A receiver MUST close the connection with an error of type FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR if the sender violates the advertised connection or stream data limits

facts.summary: A sender that has used up its limit is blocked and SHOULD signal it with STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED.
facts.quote: If a sender has sent data up to the limit, it will be unable to send new data and is considered blocked. A sender SHOULD send a STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED frame to indicate to the receiver that it has data to write but is blocked by flow control limits.

facts.summary: Blocked senders need not send blocked frames, so a receiver MUST NOT wait for STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED before raising limits.
facts.quote: A blocked sender is not required to send STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED frames. Therefore, a receiver MUST NOT wait for a STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED frame before sending a MAX_STREAM_DATA or MAX_DATA frame; doing so could result in the sender being blocked for the rest of the connection.

facts.summary: Packet loss can leave gaps in the receive buffer that keep the application from consuming data and freeing buffer space.
facts.quote: Packet loss can cause gaps in the receive buffer, preventing the application from consuming data and freeing up receive buffer space.

facts.summary: Integer transport parameters default to 0 when absent unless stated otherwise.
facts.quote: Transport parameters have a default value of 0 if the transport parameter is absent, unless otherwise stated.

facts.summary: The initial per-stream limit parameters act like a MAX_STREAM_DATA on every new stream of that type; if a parameter is absent, those streams start with a limit of 0.
facts.quote: If present, transport parameters that set initial per-stream flow control limits (initial_max_stream_data_bidi_local, initial_max_stream_data_bidi_remote, and initial_max_stream_data_uni) are equivalent to sending a MAX_STREAM_DATA frame (Section 19.10) on every stream of the corresponding type immediately after opening. If the transport parameter is absent, streams of that type start with a flow control limit of 0.

facts.summary: RFC 9114 says HTTP/2's multiplexing is invisible to TCP loss recovery, so one lost or reordered packet stalls all active transactions, affected or not.
facts.quote: HTTP/2 ([HTTP/2]) introduced a binary framing and multiplexing layer to improve latency without modifying the transport layer. However, because the parallel nature of HTTP/2's multiplexing is not visible to TCP's loss recovery mechanisms, a lost or reordered packet causes all active transactions to experience a stall regardless of whether that transaction was directly impacted by the lost packet.

facts.summary: QUIC provides reliability per stream but congestion control across the whole connection.
facts.quote: By providing reliability at the stream level and congestion control across the entire connection, QUIC has the capability to improve the performance of HTTP compared to a TCP mapping.

facts.summary: HTTP/3 relies on QUIC for reliable, in-order delivery per stream.
facts.quote: HTTP/3 relies on QUIC to provide confidentiality and integrity protection of data; peer authentication; and reliable, in-order, per-stream delivery.

facts.summary: Each HTTP/3 request-response pair uses one QUIC stream, and RFC 9114 states that a blocked or lossy stream does not stop progress on other streams.
facts.quote: Each request-response pair consumes a single QUIC stream. Streams are independent of each other, so one stream that is blocked or suffers packet loss does not prevent progress on other streams.

facts.summary: RFC 9114 says QPACK gives the encoder some control over how much head-of-line blocking compression causes, trading compression efficiency against latency.
facts.quote: [QPACK] describes a variation of HPACK that gives an encoder some control over how much head-of-line blocking can be caused by compression. This allows an encoder to balance compression efficiency with latency.

facts.summary: Transport parameters MUST let the peer open at least three unidirectional streams (control plus two QPACK streams) and SHOULD give each at least 1,024 bytes of flow-control credit.
facts.quote: Each endpoint needs to create at least one unidirectional stream for the HTTP control stream. QPACK requires two additional unidirectional streams, and other extensions might require further streams. Therefore, the transport parameters sent by both clients and servers MUST allow the peer to create at least three unidirectional streams. These transport parameters SHOULD also provide at least 1,024 bytes of flow-control credit to each unidirectional stream.

facts.summary: The critical unidirectional streams (HTTP control stream, QPACK encoder and decoder streams) SHOULD be created first, because the peer need not grant more credit if initial credit is used up beforehand.
facts.quote: Note that an endpoint is not required to grant additional credits to create more unidirectional streams if its peer consumes all the initial credits before creating the critical unidirectional streams. Endpoints SHOULD create the HTTP control stream as well as the unidirectional streams required by mandatory extensions (such as the QPACK encoder and decoder streams) first, and then create additional streams as allowed by their peer.

facts.summary: The sender MUST NOT close the control stream; if either control stream is closed at any time, it is a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM.
facts.quote: The sender MUST NOT close the control stream, and the receiver MUST NOT request that the sender close the control stream. If either control stream is closed at any point, this MUST be treated as a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM.

facts.summary: Since the control stream manages other streams, endpoints SHOULD give enough flow-control credit to keep the peer's control stream from blocking.
facts.quote: Because the contents of the control stream are used to manage the behavior of other streams, endpoints SHOULD provide enough flow-control credit to keep the peer's control stream from becoming blocked.

facts.summary: H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM has code 0x0104 and means a stream the HTTP/3 connection requires was closed or reset.
facts.quote: H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM (0x0104): A stream required by the HTTP/3 connection was closed or reset.

facts.summary: HTTP/2 gives an absolute ordering of frames across all streams, while QUIC guarantees order only within each stream, so HTTP/3 breaks frame types that assume cross-stream order.
facts.quote: Many of the differences arise from the fact that HTTP/2 provides an absolute ordering between frames across all streams, while QUIC provides this guarantee on each stream only. As a result, if a frame type makes assumptions that frames from different streams will still be received in the order sent, HTTP/3 will break them.

facts.summary: HPACK assumes in-order delivery: encoded field sections must be decoded in the order encoded to keep dynamic state in sync. QPACK instead makes all table changes on one unidirectional stream, and field-carrying frames only reference table state.
facts.quote: HPACK was designed with the assumption of in-order delivery. A sequence of encoded field sections must arrive (and be decoded) at an endpoint in the same order in which they were encoded. This ensures that the dynamic state at the two endpoints remains in sync. … Because this total ordering is not provided by QUIC, HTTP/3 uses a modified version of HPACK, called QPACK. QPACK uses a single unidirectional stream to make all modifications to the dynamic table, ensuring a total order of updates. All frames that contain encoded fields merely reference the table state at a given time without modifying it.

facts.summary: In HTTP/2 only DATA payload is flow controlled; in HTTP/3 all frame headers and payloads are, because every frame travels on a QUIC stream.
facts.quote: HTTP/2 specifies a stream flow-control mechanism. Although all HTTP/2 frames are delivered on streams, only the DATA frame payload is subject to flow control. QUIC provides flow control for stream data and all HTTP/3 frame types defined in this document are sent on streams. Therefore, all frame headers and payload are subject to flow control.

facts.summary: HTTP/3 has no CONTINUATION frame; larger HEADERS and PUSH_PROMISE frames are allowed instead.
facts.quote: CONTINUATION frames do not exist in HTTP/3; instead, larger HEADERS/PUSH_PROMISE frames than HTTP/2 are permitted.

loc.heading: A.2.5. Comparison of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Frame Types

facts.summary: RFC 9204 states that HPACK used over HTTP/3 would cause head-of-line blocking of field sections because it assumes a total ordering of frames across all streams.
facts.quote: HTTP/2 uses HPACK ([RFC7541]) for compression of the header and trailer sections. If HPACK were used for HTTP/3 ([HTTP/3]), it would induce head-of-line blocking for field sections due to built-in assumptions of a total ordering across frames on all streams.

facts.summary: QPACK is redesigned to stay correct under out-of-order delivery and lets implementations trade head-of-line blocking against compression ratio, aiming for HPACK-like ratio with much less blocking.
facts.quote: QPACK reuses core concepts from HPACK, but is redesigned to allow correctness in the presence of out-of-order delivery, with flexibility for implementations to balance between resilience against head-of-line blocking and optimal compression ratio. The design goals are to closely approach the compression ratio of HPACK with substantially less head-of-line blocking under the same loss conditions.

facts.summary: Static-table references and literals never risk head-of-line blocking; dynamic-table references risk it until the encoder has an acknowledgment that the entry reached the decoder.
facts.quote: References to the static table and literal representations do not require any dynamic state and never risk head-of-line blocking. References to the dynamic table risk head-of-line blocking if the encoder has not received an acknowledgment indicating the entry is available at the decoder.

facts.summary: Because QUIC does not order data across streams, a decoder can see a reference to a dynamic-table entry it has not yet received.
facts.quote: Because QUIC does not guarantee order between data on different streams, a decoder might encounter a representation that references a dynamic table entry that it has not yet received.

facts.summary: A stream is QPACK-blocked when an encoded field section's Required Insert Count is greater than the decoder's Insert Count.
facts.quote: When the decoder receives an encoded field section with a Required Insert Count greater than its own Insert Count, the stream cannot be processed immediately and is considered "blocked"

facts.summary: The decoder sets the upper bound with SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS; the encoder MUST keep the number of streams that could block within it at all times, and a decoder seeing more MUST treat it as QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.
facts.quote: The decoder specifies an upper bound on the number of streams that can be blocked using the SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS setting; see Section 5. An encoder MUST limit the number of streams that could become blocked to the value of SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS at all times. If a decoder encounters more blocked streams than it promised to support, it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.

facts.summary: Referencing in-transit entries can improve compression but may block on loss or reordering; referencing only acknowledged entries avoids blocking, at the cost of larger literals that can block the encoder on congestion or flow control.
facts.quote: An encoder can decide whether to risk having a stream become blocked. If permitted by the value of SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS, compression efficiency can often be improved by referencing dynamic table entries that are still in transit, but if there is loss or reordering, the stream can become blocked at the decoder. An encoder can avoid the risk of blocking by only referencing dynamic table entries that have been acknowledged, but this could mean using literals. Since literals make the encoded field section larger, this can result in the encoder becoming blocked on congestion or flow-control limits.

facts.summary: Flow-control credit on the encoder stream and on request streams can depend on each other and deadlock; to avoid it, an encoder SHOULD NOT write an instruction without enough stream and connection credit for the whole instruction.
facts.quote: A decoder might stop issuing flow-control credit on the stream that carries an encoded field section until the necessary updates are received on the encoder stream. If the granting of flow-control credit on the encoder stream (or the connection as a whole) depends on the consumption and release of data on the stream carrying the encoded field section, a deadlock might result. … To avoid these deadlocks, an encoder SHOULD NOT write an instruction unless sufficient stream and connection flow-control credit is available for the entire instruction.

facts.summary: Unlike HPACK, QPACK sends encoded field sections and the encoder-stream instructions that change the dynamic table on separate streams.
facts.quote: Note that encoded field sections and encoder stream instructions arrive on separate streams. This is unlike HPACK, where encoded field sections (header blocks) can contain instructions that modify the dynamic table, and there is no dedicated stream of HPACK instructions.

facts.summary: While a stream is blocked, its encoded data SHOULD stay counted in that stream's flow-control window; the stream unblocks once the Insert Count reaches the Required Insert Count of every field section being read.
facts.quote: While blocked, encoded field section data SHOULD remain in the blocked stream's flow-control window. This data is unusable until the stream becomes unblocked, and releasing the flow control prematurely makes the decoder vulnerable to memory exhaustion attacks. A stream becomes unblocked when the Insert Count becomes greater than or equal to the Required Insert Count for all encoded field sections the decoder has started reading from the stream.

facts.summary: The QPACK encoder and decoder streams MUST NOT be closed; closing either is a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM.
facts.quote: The sender MUST NOT close either of these streams, and the receiver MUST NOT request that the sender close either of these streams. Closure of either unidirectional stream type MUST be treated as a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM.

facts.summary: SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY has identifier 0x01 and default zero; it is the counterpart of HTTP/2's SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE.
facts.quote: SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY (0x01): The default value is zero. See Section 3.2 for usage. This is the equivalent of the SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE from HTTP/2.

facts.summary: SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS has identifier 0x07 and default zero.
facts.quote: SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS (0x07): The default value is zero.

facts.summary: QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED has code 0x0200 and means the decoder cannot interpret an encoded field section.
facts.quote: QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED (0x0200): The decoder failed to interpret an encoded field section and is not able to continue decoding that field section.

facts.summary: Data held back by flow control is outside the dynamic-table memory limit; implementations should limit unsent data, especially on the decoder stream.
facts.quote: While the negotiated limit on the dynamic table size accounts for much of the memory that can be consumed by a QPACK implementation, data that cannot be immediately sent due to flow control is not affected by this limit. Implementations should limit the size of unsent data, especially on the decoder stream where flexibility to choose what to send is limited.

conflicts.topic: does packet loss on one QUIC stream leave other HTTP/3 streams unaffected?
conflicts.note: RFC 9114 overview states streams are independent; RFC 9000 adds that a lost packet carrying data of several streams blocks all of them

conflicts.topic: can one HTTP/3 stream be held up by data on another stream?
conflicts.note: RFC 9114 overview drops the QPACK case in which a request stream blocks until encoder-stream inserts arrive (Required Insert Count greater than Insert Count)

conflicts.topic: who controls how much head-of-line blocking QPACK causes
conflicts.note: RFC 9114 credits the encoder with control; RFC 9204 makes the decoder's SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS (default zero) the cap the encoder MUST stay within

conflicts.topic: is QUIC stream delivery always in order?
conflicts.note: RFC 9114 says QUIC provides in-order per-stream delivery; RFC 9000 requires the ability to deliver in order but lets implementations MAY offer out-of-order delivery
